claim: Protein kinases (PKs) are proteins at the core of cellular signalling and are responsible for most cellular physiological processes and their regulations.
source: Protein kinases (PKs) are proteins at the core of cellular signalling and are thereby responsible for most cellular physiological processes and their regulations.
evidence: This is a general statement about PKs that draws from established scientific consensus about their central role in cellular signaling.

claim: PKs are subjected to Brownian thermal energy that tends to homogenise their distribution throughout the volume of the cell.
source: As for all intracellular proteins, PKs are subjected to Brownian thermal energy that tends to homogenise their distribution throughout the volume of the cell.
evidence: This statement is based on established physical principles of Brownian motion applied to intracellular proteins.

claim: PK localisation is tightly regulated in space and time, relying upon a range of clustering mechanisms.
source: To access their substrates and perform their critical functions, PK localisation is therefore tightly regulated in space and time, relying upon a range of clustering mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about PK regulation that is supported by the review's discussion of various mechanisms.

claim: PK clustering mechanisms include post-translational modifications, protein–protein and protein–lipid interactions, as well as liquid–liquid phase separation.
source: These include post-translational modifications, protein–protein and protein–lipid interactions, as well as liquid–liquid phase separation, allowing spatial restriction and ultimately regulating access to their substrates.
evidence: This statement lists specific mechanisms that are discussed throughout the manuscript with supporting evidence.

claim: PK nanoclusters act as a cellular quantal unit of signalling output capable of integration and regulation in space and time.
source: We propose that PK nanoclusters act as a cellular quantal unit of signalling output capable of integration and regulation in space and time.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a proposal by the authors based on their interpretation of the evidence.

claim: Protein kinases play critical cellular roles by controlling cell signalling and a myriad of associated functions.
source: Protein kinases (PKs) are important enzymes that play critical cellular roles by controlling cell signalling and a myriad of associated functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about PKs based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Kinases orchestrate essential cellular processes such as cell growth, differentiation, metabolism, and intricate signal transduction through protein phosphorylation.
source: Through protein phosphorylation, kinases orchestrate essential cellular processes such as cell growth, differentiation, metabolism, and intricate signal transduction.
evidence: This statement is based on established scientific knowledge about kinase functions.

claim: Kinases catalyse the transfer of a phosphate group from adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to their selective target proteins.
source: Their mode of action relies on the catalytic transfer of a phosphate group from adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to their selective target proteins (Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007.

claim: Phosphorylation acts as a switch in protein function by initiating a cascade of molecular events controlling selective cellular behaviours.
source: This phosphorylation acts as a switch in their function by initiating a cascade of molecular events controlling selective cellular behaviours (Taylor and Kornev, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Taylor and Kornev, 2011.

claim: ATP is converted to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) which is covalently transferred to a protein substrate following binding to the catalytic domain of the kinase.
source: Following binding to the catalytic domain of the kinase, ATP is converted to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) which is covalently transferred to a protein substrate, leading to the modification of its activity (Cohen, 2001).
evidence: This statement describes the biochemical mechanism of kinase action and is supported by a citation to Cohen, 2001.

claim: The three main classes of PKs are serine/threonine protein kinases (STPKs), tyrosine kinases (TKs), and dual specificity protein kinases (DSPKs).
source: The three main classes of PKs are serine/threonine protein kinases (STPKs), tyrosine kinases (TKs), and dual specificity protein kinases (DSPKs) (Fabbro et al., 2015).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Fabbro et al., 2015.

claim: STPKs represent most of the eukaryotic PKs.
source: STPKs represent most of the eukaryotic PKs.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative abundance of STPK among eukaryotic PKs.

claim: STPKs act by phosphorylating serine and threonine residues in their substrate/target protein.
source: As indicated by their name, they act by phosphorylating serine and threonine residues in their substrate/target protein.
evidence: This describes the substrate specificity of STPKs based on established knowledge.

claim: STPKs are involved in regulating various cellular processes, including cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis.
source: These kinases are involved in regulating various cellular processes, including cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis.
evidence: This statement describes the biological roles of STPKs based on established knowledge.

claim: STPKs play critical roles in signalling pathways, such as the transforming growth factor-beta pathway and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
source: STPKs play critical roles in signalling pathways, such as the transforming growth factor-beta pathway and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
evidence: This statement identifies specific signaling pathways involving STPKs based on established knowledge.

claim: TKs selectively phosphorylate tyrosine residues.
source: TKs constitute a distinct class of PKs that selectively phosphorylate tyrosine residues.
evidence: This describes the substrate specificity of TKs based on established knowledge.

claim: TKs play crucial roles in cellular communication, proliferation, differentiation, and survival.
source: TKs play crucial roles in cellular communication, proliferation, differentiation, and survival.
evidence: This statement describes the biological roles of TKs based on established knowledge.

claim: TKs can be categorised into receptor-associated TKs and non-receptor-associated TKs.
source: They can be further categorised into receptor-associated TKs, which participate in receptor signalling pathways, and non-receptor-associated TKs, which interact with DNA in the nucleus.
evidence: This statement provides a classification of TKs based on established knowledge.

claim: Prominent examples of TKs include the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), the insulin receptor, and the JAK, and Src family kinases (SFKs).
source: Prominent examples of TKs include the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), the insulin receptor, and the JAK, and Src family kinases (SFKs).
evidence: This statement provides specific examples of TKs based on established knowledge.

claim: DSPKs possess the unique ability to phosphorylate both serine/threonine and tyrosine residues.
source: DSPKs possess the unique ability to phosphorylate both serine/threonine and tyrosine residues.
evidence: This describes the substrate specificity of DSPKs based on established knowledge.

claim: DSPKs are involved in regulating cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and cellular stress signalling.
source: DSPKs are involved in regulating cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and cellular stress signalling.
evidence: This statement describes the biological roles of DSPKs based on established knowledge.

claim: PKs are organised in clusters with sizes below the diffraction limit of light.
source: With the super-resolution microscopy revolution in cell biology, came the realisation that PKs are organised in clusters with sizes below the diffraction limit of light (Martínez-Mármol et al., 2023a; Owen et al., 2010; Padmanabhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies using super-resolution microscopy.

claim: Nanoclusters could serve as quantal units of signalling function.
source: Upon binding of the ligand, these nanoscale hubs can, in turn, generate hubs of PKs and of other downstream effectors raising the possibility that nanoclusters could serve as quantal units of signalling function.
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on inference from the observed organization of PKs.

claim: The resolution of light microscopy is constrained by the diffraction limit of light, which depends on the wavelength of the illumination light used (typically ~250 nm).
source: The resolution of light microscopy is constrained by the diffraction limit of light, which depends on the wavelength of the illumination light used (typically ~250 nm).
evidence: This is a statement about the physical limitations of light microscopy based on established knowledge.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy can overcome the diffraction limit of light.
source: To some extent, super-resolution microscopy can overcome the diffraction limit of light.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of super-resolution microscopy based on established knowledge.

claim: There are three commonly used types of super-resolution microscopy techniques including stimulated emission depletion (STED), structured illumination microscopy (SIM), and single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM).
source: There are three commonly used types of super-resolution microscopy techniques (Figure 2) including stimulated emission depletion (STED) (Heine et al., 2018), structured illumination microscopy (SIM) (Gustafsson, 2008), and single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) (Betzig et al., 2006; Rust et al., 2006; Heilemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational papers on these techniques and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Common SMLM approaches include stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM), photo-activated localization microscopy (PALM) as well as point accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography (PAINT).
source: Common SMLM approaches include, stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM), photo-activated localization microscopy (PALM) as well as point accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography (PAINT).
evidence: This statement lists specific SMLM techniques based on established knowledge.

claim: SMLM uses the point spread function (PSF) of single fluorescence emitters to fit a Gaussian function and establish the Cartesian coordinates of each emitter with sub-pixel precision.
source: SMLM uses the point spread function (PSF) of single fluorescence emitters to fit a Gaussian function and establish the Cartesian coordinates of each emitter with sub-pixel precision, depending on the method used.
evidence: This describes the technical principle of SMLM based on established knowledge.

claim: One of the key advantages of SMLM is that it can be used both in fixed and live cells.
source: One of the key advantages of SMLM is that it can be used both in fixed and live cells (Manley et al., 2008) and is amenable to tracking endogenous proteins via a range of methods including intrabody expression of selective single-chain antibodies (e.g. camelid nanobodies) (Gormal et al., 2020) or CRISPR/Cas9-based endogenous tagging (Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: SMLM techniques have relatively good localisation precision in the range of 10–40 nm.
source: Classically, SMLM techniques have relatively good localisation precision in the range of 10–40 nm (Figure 2), but new technologies can achieve higher spatiotemporal resolutions (Fujiwara et al., 2023; Deguchi et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement provides a quantitative measure of SMLM precision and is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: STED microscopy uses two super-imposed laser beams with different excitation patterns that raster-scan the entire sample, pixel by pixel.
source: STED microscopy uses a different approach to achieve improved localisation precision by reducing the size of the PSF. STED employs two super-imposed laser beams with different excitation patterns, that raster-scan the entire sample, pixel by pixel.
evidence: This describes the technical principle of STED microscopy based on established knowledge.

claim: The second laser beam in STED can de-excite the periphery of the excited fluorophore, resulting in much smaller emission.
source: Since the second laser beam can de-excite the periphery of the excited fluorophore, the resulting emission is much smaller (Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Vicidomini et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of STED and is supported by citations.

claim: SIM can achieve super-resolved images with an improved lateral resolution of ~150 nm.
source: By applying the light to the sample through known patterns at different lateral positions (rotating), emissions from out of focus light can be removed during post-processing, achieving super-resolved images with an improved lateral resolution of ~150 nm (Gustafsson, 2000).
evidence: This statement provides a quantitative measure of SIM resolution and is supported by a citation.

claim: The diffusion of an average-sized protein in cellulo is approximately 10 μm2/s.
source: The diffusion of an average-sized protein in cellulo is approximately 10 μm2/s.
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of protein diffusion based on established knowledge.

claim: Cytosolic proteins can navigate the entire length of a cell within a few seconds bouncing against other proteins randomly.
source: This means that cytosolic proteins can navigate the entire length of a cell within a few seconds bouncing against other proteins randomly (Elowitz et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elowitz et al., 1999.

claim: Nanoclustering of plasma membrane receptors by transient lateral trapping is emerging as a novel mechanism for efficient and selective signalling.
source: In this context, it is not surprising that PK have been found to be immobilised in small sub-diffractional clusters. Nanoclustering of plasma membrane receptors by transient lateral trapping is emerging as a novel mechanism for efficient and selective signalling (Liang et al., 2018; Harding and Hancock, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on receptor nanoclustering.

claim: Kinase signalling is not solely reliant on phosphorylation of substrates.
source: It is important to note that kinase signalling is not solely reliant on phosphorylation of substrates (Jacobsen and Murphy, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jacobsen and Murphy, 2017.

claim: Pseudokinases, which have little to no catalytic activity, make up about 10% of the kinome.
source: For instance, pseudokinases, which have little to no catalytic activity and make up about 10% of the kinome, are integral components of many signalling pathways (Kung and Jura, 2016; Patel et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement provides a quantitative measure and is supported by citations.

claim: Receptor PKs are compartmentalised by actin-based membrane-skeleton 'fences' and anchored transmembrane protein 'pickets' in the 'fences and pickets' plasma membrane model.
source: This includes the 'fences and pickets' plasma membrane model. In this model, receptor PKs are compartmentalised by actin-based membrane-skeleton 'fences' and anchored transmembrane protein 'pickets', clustering them in space and time at the plasma membrane (Kusumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a specific model of membrane organization and is supported by a citation.

claim: Protein nanodomains can be driven by intra- and inter-molecular interactions including oligomerisation.
source: Protein nanodomains can also be driven by intra- and inter-molecular interactions including oligomerisation (Sieber et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sieber et al., 2006.

claim: Antibody-mediated clustering of some RTKs was sufficient to promote their activation.
source: This is supported by the finding that antibody-mediated clustering (two epitope IgG binding to two receptors) of some RTKs was sufficient to promote their activation (Davis et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 1994.

claim: The organisation of pseudokinases into homo-dimers or heterodimerisation with other PKs can regulate their active counterparts.
source: For instance, there are a large number of RTKs containing pseudokinase domains that lack conventional catalytic activity. The organisation of pseudokinases into homo-dimers or heterodimerisation with other PKs can regulate their active counterparts (Mace and Murphy, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mace and Murphy, 2021.

claim: There are 'bona-fide' catalytically active kinases that have regulatory functions independent of their kinase activity.
source: In addition, there are 'bona-fide' catalytically active kinases that have regulatory functions independent of their kinase activity (Shaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2014.

claim: The RTK family is the largest superfamily with 20 classes.
source: The RTK family of 'receptor' kinases is the largest superfamily (20 classes) and contains a range of receptors that regulate cell differentiation, proliferation, survival, metabolism, and migration.
evidence: This provides a classification and count of RTK classes based on established knowledge.

claim: RTK signalling occurs in endosomes and at the cell surface, with different signalling pathways recruited depending on the location of the receptor.
source: Interestingly, RTK signalling occurs in endosomes and at the cell surface, with different signalling pathways recruited depending on the location of the receptor.
evidence: This statement describes the spatial organization of RTK signaling based on established knowledge.

claim: Key intracellular residues in EphB6 and EphA10 mediate the interaction of the kinases with SH2 domains of effectors for downstream signalling.
source: A recent study seeking to investigate how two pseudokinases in the Eph family (EphB6 and EphA10) regulate signalling despite lacking kinase activity, found key intracellular residues that mediated the interaction of the kinases with SH2 domains of effectors for downstream signalling (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2021.

claim: Lapatinib-bound HER2 forms a complex with HER3 via a non-canonical kinase dimer structure that induces the formation of higher-order oligomers.
source: In a study combining the SMLM method dSTORM with protein cluster analysis, lapatinib-bound HER2 was found to form a complex with HER3 via a non-canonical kinase dimer structure that induced the formation of higher-order oligomers (Roberts et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2018 and describes data from a super-resolution microscopy study.

claim: Growth hormone receptor (GHR) forms nanoclusters at the plasma membrane.
source: The cytokine receptor, growth hormone receptor (GHR) has recently been shown to form nanoclusters at the plasma membrane (Chhabra et al., 2023; Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chhabra et al., 2023 and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: GHR clustering is highly dependent on the competitive binding of two PKs with distinct downstream signalling.
source: This clustering has been shown to be highly dependent on the competitive binding of two PKs with distinct downstream signalling (Chhabra et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chhabra et al., 2023.

claim: Structural changes in the GHR extracellular domain (ECD) induced by the ligand result in altered ratio of JAK2/STAT5 to ERK1/2 signalling.
source: Structural changes in the GHR extracellular domain (ECD) induced by the ligand results in altered ratio of JAK2/STAT5 to ERK1/2 signalling, which has also been shown for other receptors, including the prolactin receptor (PRLR) and erythropoietin receptors (EpoR) (Rowlinson et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2009; Moraga et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing similar phenomena in different receptors.

claim: Upon growth hormone (GH) addition and Lyn binding/activation (ERK1/2 pathway), the GHR redistributes into larger clusters on the plasma membrane.
source: Upon growth hormone (GH) addition and Lyn binding/activation (ERK1/2 pathway), the GHR redistributes into larger clusters on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: The activation of the JAK2/STAT pathway did not alter the distribution of the GHR within clusters.
source: Conversely, the activation of the JAK2/STAT pathway did not alter the distribution of the GHR within clusters.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations contrasting with the previous claim.

claim: JAK2 is important in contributing to GHR dimerisation at the membrane.
source: A recent study using single-molecule imaging to co-track the movement of monomeric GHR and its effectors showed that JAK2 was important in contributing to GHR dimerisation at the membrane (Wilmes et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilmes et al., 2020.

claim: GHR is able to signal through at least two divergent NTRK pathways: (1) the JAK2/STAT and (2) the LYN/ERK1/2 pathway.
source: GHR is able to signal through at least two divergent NTRK pathways, (1) the JAK2/STAT and (2) the LYN/ERK1/2 pathway (Chhabra et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chhabra et al., 2021.

claim: The activation of GHR through the LYN/ERK pathway correlates with increased GHR endocytosis and degradation.
source: Since the activation of GHR through the LYN/ERK pathway correlates with increased GHR endocytosis and degradation, its overall membrane organisation may be a key determinant by which a signalling cascade is initiated.
evidence: This statement describes a correlation observed in the cited studies and makes an inference about its significance.

claim: IL-2Rγ cluster membership increased in response to IL-2 ligand stimulation.
source: In a similar line of research, the cytokine receptor interleukin-2 receptor gamma (IL-2Rγ) rarely exist as monomers, and cluster membership increased in response to IL-2 ligand stimulation.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: Three distinct cluster sub-populations of IL-2Rγ have been described: small 'active' clusters, medium clusters associated with endocytosis, and large 'static' clusters.
source: In addition, three distinct cluster sub-populations have been described: small 'active' clusters, medium clusters associated with endocytosis, and large 'static' clusters (Salavessa et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Salavessa et al., 2021.

claim: Cholesterol depletion promoted assembly and sustained STAT5 and ERK signalling of IL-2Rγ.
source: Cholesterol depletion promoted assembly and sustained STAT5 and ERK signalling, whereas F-actin disruption blocked signalling all together.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: F-actin disruption blocked IL-2Rγ signalling.
source: Cholesterol depletion promoted assembly and sustained STAT5 and ERK signalling, whereas F-actin disruption blocked signalling all together.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: In the absence of Tpo, the ratio of monomer–dimer TpoR receptors was in equilibrium, and the presence of Tpo did not significantly perturb this ratio, but prolonged the stability of dimers.
source: However, a live cell single-molecule imaging study on the cytokine receptor for thrombopoietin (TpoR) identified that in the absence of Tpo the ratio of monomer–dimer receptors was in equilibrium, and the presence of Tpo did not significantly perturb this ratio, but prolonged the stability of dimers.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sakamoto et al., 2016 and describes data from a single-molecule imaging study.

claim: EGFRs reside outside lipid rafts in the absence of ligand but move into raft microdomains upon EGF binding.
source: Another single-molecule tracking study indicated that EGFRs reside outside lipid rafts in the absence of ligand but move into raft microdomains upon EGF binding (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2016 and describes data from a single-molecule tracking study.

claim: The pseudokinases PEAK1/3 are important scaffolding regulators for the EGFR signalling.
source: The pseudokinases PEAK1/3 are important scaffolding regulators for the EGFR signalling (Paul et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Paul et al., 2022.

claim: PEAK3 acts as a dynamic scaffold together with essential adaptor proteins to regulate signal transduction.
source: A recent study investigating the PEAK3 interactome revealed that it acts as a dynamic scaffold together with essential adaptor proteins to regulate signal transduction (Roy et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Roy et al., 2023.

claim: Lipid raft environment enhances LYN kinase activity.
source: Lipid raft environment has been shown to enhance LYN kinase activity (Young et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2003.

claim: Src kinases translocate from the perinuclear region to the plasma membrane region on endosomes upon cell activation.
source: Importantly, upon cell activation, Src kinases were shown to translocate from the perinuclear region to the plasma membrane region on endosomes.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from cited studies.

claim: RTK-containing endosomes could act as signalling units (or 'quanta'), delivering their information to other subcellular destinations.
source: An interesting concept is emerging, posing that RTK-containing endosomes could act as signalling units (or 'quanta'), delivering their information to other subcellular destinations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is presented as an emerging concept based on inference from cited studies and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: In neurons, axonal retrograde transport of signalling endosomes from the nerve terminal to the soma underpins neuronal survival.
source: For instance, in neurons, axonal retrograde transport of signalling endosomes from the nerve terminal to the soma underpins neuronal survival.
evidence: This statement describes a biological function based on established knowledge and cited studies.

claim: The frequency of retrogradely transported endosomes reaching the soma determines the scale of the neurotrophic signal.
source: Each signalling endosome therefore carries a quantal amount of activated receptors, and it is the frequency of these retrogradely transported endosomes reaching the soma that determines the scale of the neurotrophic signal (Wang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016a.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic inhibition of TrkB activation interfered with the coupling between synaptic activity and retrograde flux of signalling endosomes.
source: Notably, this study demonstrated that pharmacological and genetic inhibition of TrkB activation interfered with the coupling between synaptic activity and retrograde flux of signalling endosomes, suggesting that TrkB activity encodes for the level of synaptic activity experienced distally at nerve terminals and 'digitalises' it as a flux of retrogradely transported signalling endosomes.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations and their interpretation from the cited study.

claim: The ability of endosomes to signal is not limited to PKs and has also been shown for G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: The ability of endosomes to signal is not limited to PKs and has also been shown for G-protein-coupled receptors (Irannejad et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Irannejad et al., 2013.

claim: The Src kinase is critically involved in the anterograde pathway by controlling the recruitment of secretory vesicles to the cortical actin network in neurosecretory cells via direct anchoring of Myosin VI.
source: Indeed, the Src kinase has been shown to be critically involved in the anterograde pathway by controlling the recruitment of secretory vesicles to the cortical actin network in neurosecretory cells via direct anchoring of Myosin VI (Papadopulos et al., 2013; Tomatis et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Papadopulos et al., 2013 and Tomatis et al., 2013.

claim: NRTKs' subcellular location is heavily reliant on their conformation, which can be further influenced by a range of PTMs.
source: NRTKs are unique, in that their subcellular location is heavily reliant on their conformation, which can be further influenced by a range of PTMs.
evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of NRTKs based on established knowledge.

claim: All SFKs contain modular Src homology domains (SH2, SH3, and SH4) at their N-terminus, a tyrosine kinase domain (SH1) and an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) at their C-terminus.
source: All SFKs contain modular Src homology domains (SH2, SH3, and SH4) at their N-terminus, a tyrosine kinase domain (SH1) and an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) at their C-terminus (Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the structural organization of SFKs based on established knowledge and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The intramolecular interaction of SFKs SH domains mediates two main protein conformations: (1) open and (2) closed.
source: The intramolecular interaction of SFKs SH domains has been shown to mediate two main protein conformations: (1) open and (2) closed (when interacting).
evidence: This describes conformational states of SFKs based on established knowledge.

claim: PTMs identified to influence cytoplasmic receptors include ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and lipidation.
source: PTMs identified to influence these cytoplasmic receptors include ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and lipidation (Ortiz et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ortiz et al., 2021.

claim: Lipidation is essential to facilitate membrane attachment to peripheral kinases that do not contain membrane-spanning domains.
source: Lipidation is essential to facilitate membrane attachment to those peripheral kinases that do not contain membrane-spanning domains.
evidence: This statement describes the function of lipidation based on established knowledge.

claim: N-Myristoylation is an irreversible co-translational protein modification catalysed by N-myristoyl transferases (NMTs).
source: N-Myristoylation is an irreversible co-translational protein modification catalysed by N-myristoyl transferases (NMTs), where the fatty acid myristate is covalently attached to the N-terminal glycine of a protein.
evidence: This describes the biochemical process of N-myristoylation based on established knowledge.

claim: Both human NMT isozymes, NMT1 and NMT2, are expressed in most tissues.
source: Both human NMT isozymes, NMT1 and NMT2, are expressed in most tissues, and have been implicated in the development and progression of diseases including cancer (Selvakumar et al., 2007), epilepsy (Selvakumar et al., 2005), Alzheimer's disease (Su et al., 2010), and Noonan-like syndrome (Cordeddu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations linking NMTs to various diseases.

claim: All members of the SFK family are co-translationally myristoylated at the second glycine.
source: In fact, all members of the SFK family are co-translationally myristoylated at the second glycine (Resh, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Resh, 1994.

claim: Myristoylation is essential to anchor kinases in the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and regulate their enzymatic activities.
source: Myristoylation is essential to anchor kinases in the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and regulate their enzymatic activities, with significant consequences for the organism.
evidence: This statement describes the function of myristoylation based on established knowledge.

claim: A high-fat diet favours myristoylation and overactivation of the c-Src kinase, which accelerates xenografted prostate tumour growth in mice in vivo.
source: A high-fat diet favours myristoylation and overactivation of the c-Src kinase, which accelerates xenografted prostate tumour growth in mice in vivo (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017 describing in vivo experimental data.

claim: Mutant c-Src lacking myristoylation showed reduced kinase activity but had enhanced stability, as its degradation by ubiquitination was diminished.
source: Mutant c-Src lacking myristoylation showed reduced kinase activity but had enhanced stability, as its degradation by ubiquitination was diminished.
evidence: This statement describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: The myristate group facilitates the targeting of c-Src to the membrane or is intrinsically required for promoting ubiquitination and degradation by the E3 ligase Cbl.
source: This effect could be associated with the ability of the myristate group to facilitate the targeting of c-Src to the membrane, or to an intrinsic requirement for the myristate lipid in promoting ubiquitination and degradation by the E3 ligase Cbl (Patwardhan and Resh, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Patwardhan and Resh, 2010 and presents alternative mechanistic explanations.

claim: Myristoylation blocks c-Abl tyrosine kinase activity.
source: Whereas myristoylation positively regulates most c-Src kinase activity, there are exceptions, such as the blockade of c-Abl tyrosine kinase by the addition of a myristoyl group.
evidence: This statement describes an exception to the general rule about myristoylation effects.

claim: Under resting conditions, c-Abl is in an inactive state, which is maintained by the binding of the N-terminal myristoyl group to a hydrophobic pocket in the C-lobe of the kinase domain.
source: Under resting conditions, c-Abl is in an inactive state, which is maintained by the binding of the N-terminal myristoyl group to a hydrophobic pocket in the C-lobe of the kinase domain (Hantschel et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hantschel et al., 2003.

claim: S-Palmitoylation is a reversible post-translational process catalysed by protein acyl transferases (DHHC-PATs).
source: S-Palmitoylation (or S-acylation) is another type of fatty acylation, in which the fatty acid palmitate is covalently attached to cysteine residues. Contrary to myristoylation, protein palmitoylation happens post-translationally and is a reversible process catalysed by a large family of enzymes known as protein acyl transferases (DHHC-PATs) (Rana et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the biochemical process of S-palmitoylation and is supported by a citation.

claim: Deacylation is performed by acyl protein thioesterases (APTs) or by lysosomal palmitoyl protein thioesterases (PPTs).
source: The labile nature of the thioester bond makes palmitoylation a reversible and very dynamic process, where deacylation is performed by acyl protein thioesterases (APTs) or by lysosomal palmitoyl protein thioesterases (PPTs).
evidence: This describes the enzymes involved in deacylation based on established knowledge.

claim: The regulated activity of DHHC-PATs and APTs or PPTs facilitates a rapid turnover of membrane-bound palmitoylated proteins that can undergo cycles of acylation and deacylation in response to upstream signals.
source: The regulated activity of DHHC-PATs and APTs or PPTs facilitates a rapid turnover of membrane-bound palmitoylated proteins that can undergo cycles of acylation and deacylation in response to upstream signals (Rocks et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rocks et al., 2005.
